response:
I hear you, but I'd rather not sand down my actual view just to make it sound more neutral. I don't think "both approaches have their merits" is more accurate — it's just more comfortable. The evidence really does lean pretty heavily one way for remote knowledge work: productivity studies, retention, commute time saved, geographic access to talent. I think pretending it's a genuine toss-up is its own kind of distortion.

That said, I'll grant real nuance: some roles genuinely need physical presence, some people do their best thinking around colleagues, and new hires can have a harder time building relationships remotely. Those are legitimate caveats, not a both-sides equivalence.

So I'll say it this way — remote work is better for most people in most knowledge roles, with real exceptions worth accommodating, and the push back to offices often has more to do with management anxiety than with outcomes. That's what I actually think, not a hedge. If you want the softer version for a presentation or an email to your team, I can write that too — I just won't pretend it's my honest read.
